title: Nvidia board preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, Journal reports
excerpt: Nvidia's board is preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang after two extramarital affairs, the Wall Street Journal reported, sending shares down about 8%.
content:
Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to remove co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday evening, after Huang had two extramarital affairs — one with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese intelligence asset, and another with a company executive who reports to him.

The board met Wednesday to discuss Huang's future, according to people familiar with the matter cited by the Journal. As of Thursday morning, the company had not announced any decision.

On Sunday, Huang acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized for violating their trust, the Journal reported. The New York Times reported Wednesday that the second affair involved an Nvidia executive who reports to Huang. The Times first reported in October 2025 about a business connection between Huang and Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the espionage questions.

The board had earlier said it was investigating whether Huang became the target of a foreign espionage effort connected to the affair. In a statement this week, the board said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" and expressed "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team."

Investors reacted sharply. Nvidia shares fell about 8 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday and were down almost 8 percent again in premarket trading Thursday, the Journal reported. The stock has lost more than $365 billion in market value since the revelations about Huang's affair surfaced. Just weeks ago, Nvidia was the world's most valuable public company, with a market capitalization above $5 trillion; the slide now threatens to drop it to No. 3, behind Microsoft, based on premarket trading.

Analysts are split on what comes next. Baird analysts wrote that Huang might have to step down, downgraded the stock to neutral and cut their price target 60 percent, to $200. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives reiterated an outperform rating with a $300 target, arguing Huang is "not replaceable" and that Nvidia's AI success is tied to him staying on as chief executive.

Prediction markets have moved fast: bettors on Polymarket put 77 percent odds on Huang leaving his position by resignation or removal by year-end, according to the Journal.

Why it matters beyond Nvidia

Huang, 63, is Nvidia's largest shareholder, owning about 3.6 percent of the company, and is widely seen as the face of the global AI arms race. Nvidia's chips power the data centers behind the artificial-intelligence boom, including the large data-center buildout underway across Texas. A sudden leadership change at the world's most valuable chipmaker would ripple through the AI supply chain, the stock market and the companies betting their futures on Nvidia hardware.

What is not yet established is whether any Nvidia secrets or national security were compromised. The board's investigation is ongoing, and the espionage question remains an allegation under review — not a finding. Readers should treat the reporting as what it is: the Journal's account, based on people familiar with the matter, and the board's own public statements.
